title: Quintilian subsidiary-question order constructor
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED, NOT SELECTED. Quintilian Institutio oratoria VII.2 and VII.5–10 insists that a complex case be divided into ordered questions: first the governing legal interpretation, then subsidiary questions, with each argument attached to its proper issue. A scope-stack constructor predicts different conclusions when issue order is changed.

source.source_span: VII.2 definite questions; VII.5–10 division and order of complex legal questions
source_facts: A definite question can concern what has been done, is being done, or is likely to be done.
Quintilian gives a complex example in which whether to follow the letter or intention of a law must precede subsidiary questions about reward, property, marriage and the particular claimant.
He compares proper arrangement to parts of a body: later questions depend on the earlier division.

duplicate_screen.checked: ideas search/duplicates Quintilian argument order/scope and route-check rhetorical issue; Cicero status card kept as a different issue-type router
duplicate_screen.difference: Cicero routes a case by constitutio; this card specifically models ordered subdivision and scope inheritance among subsidiary questions, not type selection alone.

worked_examples: OPEN_CASE(reward_claim)->CHOOSE_MODE(letter_or_intention); only then SPLIT into property, marriage, and claimant questions
reordering property before the letter/intention question changes which interpretation governs the subsidiary answer
constructor.consequence: The same later question has different admissible outputs under a changed parent interpretation, while the case identity remains. A flat list rival lets all questions answer independently and predicts order-insensitive conclusions.
constructor.smallest_test: Require two complete source cases with the same subsidiary question but opposite parent interpretation/order, and test whether the downstream answer changes.
constructor.rival: A set of independent legal questions with no scope stack; order is rhetorical presentation only.
assumptions: Question scope is represented explicitly; no target conjunction is presumed.
The legal example is source-owned and not evidence for manuscript genre.
failure_modes: Quintilian is prescribing rhetoric, so the constructor may describe exposition rather than an underlying event.
The text permits multiple questions, making exact arity uncertain.
Without independent parent/child markers, scope is not identifiable.

dependencies: Source-only rhetorical construction; no target text, word values, or Latin cipher is used.
